scope: Four retrieved ExamBase papers. No inaccessible-paper contents inferred.
counting_rule: One row is a listed question/subquestion bundle, not necessarily a single printed leaf subpart. Distinct papers are counted once per workflow. Counts are not marks or future probabilities.
priority_rule: A representative diagnostic within its workflow; multiple priority rows identify materially different branches. Does not mean solved or predicted.

workflows.title: Gas measurements → moles → composition or stoichiometry
workflows.recognition: P, V and T; gas density or flask masses; wet gas; mixture composition; a decomposing solid.
workflows.prerequisites: Moles, balanced equations, empirical formulas, mole fractions and Kelvin temperatures.
method: Write what the measured pressure represents. For gas collected over water, first use \(P_{gas}=P_{total}-P_{H_2O}\). Convert all units to match the chosen gas constant.
Use \(n=PV/(RT)\). For a fixed amount, use \(P_1V_1/T_1=P_2V_2/T_2\). For molar mass use \(M=mRT/(PV)\), with vapour mass equal to filled-flask mass minus empty-flask mass.

For composition, take a 100 g basis, turn mass percentages into mole ratios, obtain an empirical formula, and compare its mass with the gas-derived molar mass. For a mixture, calculate each component's moles, then \(P_i=x_iP_{total}\).
For a gas-producing reaction, use the balanced mole ratio before converting to solid mass or percentage. Keep the measured volume separate from a volume requested at different conditions.
workflows.traps: Mass percentages are not mole fractions. Do not use °C in gas equations or blindly subtract water vapour when the question does not describe wet collection.
workflows.check: Check that partial pressures sum to the total, formula multipliers are near integers, and a mass percentage lies between 0 and 100.

workflows.title: Ideal-gas assumptions → real-gas corrections
workflows.recognition: Kinetic-molecular postulates; high pressure or low temperature; van der Waals constants a and b.
workflows.prerequisites: Ideal-gas equation and the physical meaning of intermolecular attractions and finite molecular volume.
method: List the idealizations relevant to the question: negligible molecular volume, negligible intermolecular forces, random motion and elastic collisions.
At high pressure, excluded molecular volume becomes important; at low temperature, attractions become important relative to kinetic energy.
Use \((P+a n^2/V^2)(V-nb)=nRT\). If finding temperature, rearrange to \(T=(P+a n^2/V^2)(V-nb)/(nR)\).
Calculate the ideal-gas result separately and explain the discrepancy in terms of the two corrections, rather than assuming all real gases always have pressure below the ideal value.
workflows.traps: The pressure correction uses n²/V², not n/V; a and b must match the pressure and volume units. Avoid claiming one correction dominates at every condition.
workflows.check: As a and b approach zero, the equation must reduce to PV=nRT; V must exceed nb.

workflows.title: Temperature and mass → speed, energy or effusion
workflows.recognition: rms speed; kinetic energy per atom; two gases at the same temperature; equal-time effusion.
workflows.prerequisites: Distinguish molar mass from molecular mass and energy per mole from energy per molecule.
method: For rms speed use \(u_{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}\), with M in kg mol⁻¹ when R is in SI units. At equal temperature, the speed ratio is the inverse square-root mass ratio.
Average translational energy per molecule is \(3k_BT/2\); per mole it is \(3RT/2\). Equal temperature implies equal average translational kinetic energy, not equal speed.
For an effusion comparison at equal conditions use \(r_A/r_B=\sqrt{M_B/M_A}\). In equal times, replace rates by escaped amounts, and convert molecule counts to moles when requested.
For equal speeds at different temperatures, set T/M equal for the two gases and solve the ratio before inserting numbers.
workflows.traps: Do not invert Graham's ratio or use molar mass in g mol⁻¹ in an SI speed calculation.
workflows.check: A lighter gas must move or effuse faster at the same temperature.

workflows.title: Electron count → MO diagram → bond and magnetic properties
workflows.recognition: Diatomic molecules or ions; draw an MO diagram; compare bond order, magnetism or bond length; explain MO versus VB.
workflows.prerequisites: Atomic valence configurations, ion charges, Pauli exclusion and Hund's rule.
method: Count valence electrons for each species, adding electrons for a negative charge and subtracting for a positive charge. State whether 1s/core orbitals are omitted.

Choose the appropriate MO energy ordering. The relative σ2p and π2p ordering changes across the second period; heteronuclear atomic orbital energies are unequal. Label atomic and molecular sides, energy direction, and bonding/antibonding orbitals.
Fill from low energy upwards using Pauli and Hund. Calculate \(BO=(N_{bonding}-N_{antibonding})/2\). Count unpaired electrons for the magnetic property.

Explain related-species bond-length/strength changes through occupation of bonding or antibonding orbitals. For conceptual questions, contrast localized VB overlap with orbitals delocalized over the molecule, and constructive with destructive overlap.
workflows.traps: A single memorized orbital ordering is not valid for every species. Bond order alone is not a universal length ranking across different atom pairs. The 2022 species are NO⁺ and N₂⁺; OCR can corrupt the second label.
workflows.check: Electron totals must match the charge; paramagnetism requires at least one unpaired electron.

workflows.title: Band occupancy and band gap → electrical conductivity
workflows.recognition: Metals, silicon, magnesium, semiconductors or the formation of bands.
workflows.prerequisites: Many atomic orbitals produce closely spaced levels; electrons need accessible empty states.
method: Explain how combining orbitals from many atoms produces bands of closely spaced energy levels.
Draw occupied and available states: a partly filled band or overlapping bands for a conductor, a small gap for a semiconductor, and a large gap for an insulator.

Relate conductivity to mobile carriers and accessible states, not merely the number of valence electrons. For Mg, discuss band overlap; for intrinsic semiconductors, discuss thermal excitation across a small gap.
workflows.traps: An isolated-atom filled shell is not sufficient to declare a solid insulating. Label valence band, conduction band and gap on the sketch.
workflows.check: Your drawing must explain where a promoted or moving electron can go.

workflows.title: Gas solubility and partial pressure → Henry's-law calculation
workflows.recognition: Dissolved oxygen/nitrogen/carbon dioxide; gas volume per water volume; minimum atmospheric pressure.
workflows.prerequisites: Molarity, partial pressure and ideal-gas conversion.
method: Read the convention and units of the given Henry constant. For \(c=k_Hp\), kH has concentration/pressure units; some sources use its reciprocal.
Convert gas-volume solubility into moles using the temperature and pressure at which that gas volume is reported, then divide by solution volume. Convert mg L⁻¹ to mol L⁻¹ when needed.
Use the solute gas's partial pressure, not total air pressure. At fixed temperature, \(c_2/c_1=p_2/p_1\); in air \(p_i=y_iP\).
For gas released on heating, calculate dissolved moles before and after using the relevant solubilities, subtract them, then use PV=nRT for the released gas at its stated measurement conditions.
workflows.traps: Do not confuse the solution temperature with the reporting conditions of a quoted gas volume. Henry's constant changes with temperature. The reporting pressure in 2022 Q3(a) is not explicitly stated; record any assumption rather than inventing certainty.
workflows.check: At the same temperature a lower partial pressure must give a lower dissolved concentration.

workflows.title: Vapour pressure → mole fraction → concentration or molar mass
workflows.recognition: A nonvolatile solute; solvent vapour-pressure lowering; an unknown molar mass.
workflows.prerequisites: Moles and mole fractions, not mass fractions.
method: For an ideal solution containing a nonvolatile solute, use \(P=x_{solvent}P^*\). If solving an inverse problem, obtain x_solvent from P/P* first.
Convert the solvent mass to moles. Then \(n_{solute}=n_{solvent}(1/x_{solvent}-1)\), followed by \(M_{solute}=m_{solute}/n_{solute}\).
For a forward problem, calculate both mole amounts, form x_solvent, and multiply by the pure-solvent vapour pressure. Vapour-pressure lowering is P*−P.
workflows.traps: Mass fraction is not mole fraction. Both volatile components require a two-component Raoult calculation, not the nonvolatile-solute shortcut.
workflows.check: For a nonvolatile solute in this ideal model, 0<P<P* and mole fractions sum to 1.

workflows.title: Particle concentration → freezing, boiling or osmotic pressure
workflows.recognition: Freezing-point depression; boiling-point elevation; osmotic pressure; particle-based rankings.
workflows.prerequisites: Molality uses kilograms of solvent; molarity uses litres of solution; dissociation changes particle counts.
method: Choose the branch: \(\Delta T_f=iK_fm\), \(\Delta T_b=iK_bm\), or \(\Pi=iCRT\). Write the original pure-solvent temperature before applying the change.
For an unknown molar mass, infer molality or molarity from the measured property, then moles and M=mass/moles. For a molecular formula, compare the inferred molar mass with the elemental unit mass.
For ranking, compare i×molality under the question's dissociation assumptions. The largest particle molality gives the lowest freezing point.
For mass-percent solutions, take a 100 g solution basis and distinguish solvent mass from total solution mass.
workflows.traps: A freezing point goes down, not up. Use consistent pressure units in Π=CRT. Do not assume complete dissociation unless appropriate or explicitly stated.
workflows.check: An inferred i should be physically plausible; a non-electrolyte has i≈1 in the ideal dilute model.

workflows.title: Dissolution stoichiometry and pH → solubility
workflows.recognition: Ksp, molar solubility, common ions, fixed pH, or whether acid increases solubility.
workflows.prerequisites: Balanced dissolution equations, equilibrium products and Kw.
method: Write the dissolution equation before the Ksp expression. For a salt M_aX_b with no pre-existing ions, use [M]=a s and [X]=b s, so \(K_{sp}=(as)^a(bs)^b\).
With a common ion, include its initial concentration and the dissolution contribution before making a small-s approximation. For fixed pH obtain [H⁺], then [OH⁻] from Kw when required.
For hydroxides use their correct powers: for M(OH)₂, Ksp=[M²⁺][OH⁻]². Solubility s is not the same quantity or unit as Ksp.

For qualitative acid effects, ask whether H⁺ consumes the dissolved anion or ligand and thereby drives dissolution. Compare the anion's acid-base chemistry rather than using a blanket rule that all salts dissolve in acid.
workflows.traps: Do not set every dissolved-ion concentration equal to s. Check the approximation after calculating s and do not treat a buffered pH as changing freely.
workflows.check: Substitute the final ion concentrations back into Ksp; a common ion normally decreases solubility in the simple model.

workflows.title: Precipitation boundary → separation, amount or buffer requirement
workflows.recognition: Mix solutions; precipitate first; separate ions; maximum reagent before a second salt appears; suppress precipitation with a buffer.
workflows.prerequisites: Dilution, ionic-product expressions, stoichiometric material balances and basic buffer equilibria.
method: After mixing, calculate ion amounts and divide by the total volume. Form Qsp and compare it with Ksp: precipitation is favoured when Qsp>Ksp.
For selective precipitation, set Qsp=Ksp separately for each salt to obtain its threshold reagent-ion concentration. Compare thresholds, not bare Ksp values of differently stoichiometric salts.
At the onset of the unwanted precipitate, use its threshold reagent concentration in the first salt's Ksp to find how much target ion remains.
For the amount precipitated, impose material balances with a precipitated amount variable and the final Ksp condition. A limiting-reagent estimate may need an equilibrium residual correction.

For a buffer preventing hydroxide precipitation, derive the maximum [OH⁻] from Ksp and the diluted metal concentration, then use the NH₃/NH₄⁺ equilibrium to find required NH₄⁺. Convert ion moles to salt moles using the salt's stoichiometry.
workflows.traps: Do not forget dilution or assume 'no precipitate' merely because a salt is sparingly soluble. A buffer-control question adds an acid-base step rather than replacing the Ksp threshold.
workflows.check: The proposed separation window must exist; verify Qsp for both salts at your selected reagent concentration.

workflows.title: Complex formation → free metal-ion concentration
workflows.recognition: A metal in excess NH₃; large formation constant; free uncomplexed ion requested.
workflows.prerequisites: Formation equilibrium, ligand stoichiometry and mass balances.
method: Write \(M+qL\rightleftharpoons ML_q\) and \(K_f=[ML_q]/([M][L]^q)\). Distinguish total metal from free metal.
If Kf is large and ligand is in excess, estimate [MLq]≈total metal, but subtract q times the complex concentration from the total ligand concentration.
Calculate free metal with \([M]\approx[ML_q]/(K_f[L]_{free}^q)\), then check that it is small compared with total metal.
If solid dissolution and complexation are coupled, add the reactions and multiply their equilibrium constants; solve a single consistent mass balance.
workflows.traps: Initial ligand concentration is not necessarily free ligand concentration. The ligand exponent is q, and adding a metal salt does not mean its free-ion concentration equals total metal.
workflows.check: For 2022 Q4(c), the large-Kf approximation leaves about 1.20−4×0.20=0.40 M free NH₃, not 1.20 M.

workflows.title: Reaction data or K → Gibbs energy → direction and equilibrium
workflows.recognition: Tabulated formation data; reaction entropy/enthalpy; K, Q, spontaneity, equilibrium composition or maximum non-expansion work.
workflows.prerequisites: Balanced reactions, reaction quotients and the distinction between standard and actual conditions.
method: Balance the reaction first. For tabulated quantities use products minus reactants, including every stoichiometric coefficient. Calculate ΔH°, ΔS° or ΔG°f sums as required; convert J and kJ consistently.
Use \(\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ=-RT\ln K\). For actual conditions, write the dimensionless reaction quotient and use \(\Delta G=\Delta G^\circ+RT\ln Q=RT\ln(Q/K)\).
If Q<K the forward direction is favoured; if Q>K the reverse direction is favoured. Pure solids and pure liquids have unit activity and do not appear in Q.
For final composition set up an ICE/material-balance table and enforce Q=K. A numerical equilibrium constant does not permit setting every species equal.

Maximum useful non-expansion work delivered by a reversible process at fixed T and P is −ΔG for that process. At an already equilibrated mixture the reaction ΔG is zero; ΔG° need not be zero. State which conditions a work answer assumes.
workflows.traps: A positive ΔG° does not prohibit a forward reaction under nonstandard conditions. Do not use Celsius, forget stoichiometric powers, or call −RT ln K the actual ΔG at equilibrium.
workflows.check: Signs must agree: K>1 implies ΔG°<0; Q=K implies ΔG=0. Be explicit about the terse work wording in 2020 May Q5(ii).

workflows.title: Specified thermodynamic path → heat, work and entropy
workflows.recognition: Reversible/isothermal gas expansion; heating at constant pressure; q, w, ΔU, ΔH or ΔS.
workflows.prerequisites: First-law sign convention and heat capacities.
method: State the sign convention: ΔU=q+w with work done on the system positive. An ideal gas's U and H depend only on temperature.
For reversible isothermal expansion, \(w=-nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)\), q=−w and ΔU=ΔH=0.
For isothermal ideal-gas entropy change, \(\Delta S=nR\ln(V_2/V_1)\). For heating at fixed pressure with constant Cp, \(\Delta S=nC_{p,m}\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
For a combined ideal-gas state change, a reversible reference path gives \(\Delta S=nC_{V,m}\ln(T_2/T_1)+nR\ln(V_2/V_1)\); do not use q/T for an arbitrary irreversible process.
workflows.traps: Use natural logarithms and Kelvin. A heat capacity described as molar must be multiplied by n. Reversible and irreversible work are not interchangeable.
workflows.check: Isothermal expansion has w<0 and ΔS>0; check q+w=0.

workflows.title: Two equilibrium temperatures → van't Hoff enthalpy
workflows.recognition: Two K values at different temperatures; compare inferred ΔH° with formation-data ΔH°.
workflows.prerequisites: Natural logarithms, Kelvin and reaction enthalpy sums.
method: Label (T1,K1) and (T2,K2) explicitly and convert both temperatures to Kelvin.
Use \(\ln(K_2/K_1)=-(\Delta H^\circ/R)(1/T_2-1/T_1)\) and solve for ΔH°.

Independently calculate the reaction enthalpy from formation data and stoichiometric coefficients. Compare the two estimates and the assumption that ΔH° is approximately constant over the temperature range.
workflows.traps: Do not mix log10 with ln or invert only one ratio. Report the temperature interval and the constant-enthalpy assumption.
workflows.check: If K decreases as temperature rises, the inferred reaction enthalpy should be negative.

workflows.title: Balanced cell reaction ↔ E° ↔ ΔG° and K
workflows.recognition: A voltaic cell, standard reduction potentials, theoretical battery voltage, or K from a cell.
workflows.prerequisites: Oxidation/reduction half-equations and balanced electron transfer.
method: Write both half-reactions as reductions to compare tabulated values. Choose the cathode reduction and reverse the anode reaction; balance electron numbers to obtain n and the full cell equation.
Use \(E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}\). Multiplying a half-equation does not multiply its electrode potential.
Use \(\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ\) and \(\ln K=nFE^\circ/(RT)\). In the reverse direction, obtain ΔG° from formation data and then E°=−ΔG°/(nF).
For a cell sketch include the electrodes, solutions, external electron path and ionic connection; electrons flow externally from anode to cathode in a galvanic cell.
workflows.traps: Do not confuse the sign of an electrode potential with the electrode's name, or scale volts with reaction coefficients. n is the electron count of the balanced overall reaction.
workflows.check: A spontaneous standard cell has E°>0, ΔG°<0 and K>1. The silver-zinc cell transfers two electrons per written overall reaction.

workflows.title: Nonstandard concentrations and material balance → Nernst potential
workflows.recognition: Cell notation contains concentrations; potential as a cell runs; find concentration at a specified E.
workflows.prerequisites: Balanced cell equation, reaction quotient and logarithms.
method: Write and balance the cell reaction in the direction represented by the cell notation, then obtain E° and n.
Build Q from the balanced reaction, omitting pure solids/liquids. Use \(E=E^\circ-(RT/nF)\ln Q\), or at 298 K \(E=E^\circ-(0.05916/n)\log_{10}Q\).
If the cell runs, update both half-cell compositions using the same reaction extent and the actual solution volumes. State any equal-volume assumption if the paper omits the volumes.
For an inverse problem first solve for Q from the target E, then combine that ratio with the material balance. Assess spontaneity from the calculated E in the written direction.
workflows.traps: Do not use initial Q after the cell has run, invert Q without reversing the reaction, or apply 0.05916 at every temperature.
workflows.check: As a galvanic cell approaches equilibrium, E tends to zero and Q tends to K.

workflows.title: Molarity and density → molality
workflows.recognition: A solution is specified by molarity and density but molality is requested.
workflows.prerequisites: Mass of solution equals density times volume; solvent mass excludes the solute.
method: Take 1.000 L of solution: the molarity directly gives solute moles.
Multiply density by 1000 mL to obtain solution mass. Subtract solute moles times molar mass to obtain solvent mass.
Convert solvent mass to kilograms and calculate molality as solute moles per kg solvent.
workflows.traps: The 1 L basis is solution volume, not solvent volume. Do not divide by solution mass.
workflows.check: The inferred solvent mass must be positive and smaller than the total solution mass.

workflows.title: Temperature-dependent solubility → recrystallization explanation
workflows.recognition: State the purpose and working principle of recrystallization.
workflows.prerequisites: Solubility varies with temperature; impurities can behave differently.
method: State that the aim is purification of a solid, not chemical conversion.
Explain dissolving the impure solid in minimal suitable hot solvent, removing insoluble impurities if needed, then cooling to crystallize the desired material.
Explain why soluble impurities ideally remain in the mother liquor and why some product is lost. Identify the need for a suitable hot/cold solubility contrast.
workflows.traps: Do not claim that every impurity is automatically removed or that cooling creates more solute.
workflows.check: Your explanation must connect purification to differential solubility, not only list laboratory steps.
